items.title: Jimmy Cobb — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: She was a Southern lady. She had to go along with it too, because that’s the way it was at the time.

ctx.x: What did your mother convey to you about these rules, if anything?

She was a Southern lady. She had to go along with it too, because that’s the way it was at the time. Where she came from, her people did laundry. I remember being out in a field with a big pot with – what do you call it? – blue-in and all that stuff they put in the pot to make the clothes whiter. My aunt – my grand aunt, she used to do clothes for the whole neighborhood. The people in the neighborhood would bring their clothes, and she would wash them, iron them, and deliver them. So that was her gig. My…

the whole season. Plant the tobacco. Grow it. Then cut it. Then spear it [pronounced “spare it”]. Then hang it up in the barn to dry. Then sell it, and probably get about $300 for all that work he did. He was working his butt off for no money, but that’s all he could do, and that’s what he did.
